title: The Story of Sidi-Nouman
paragraphs: The Caliph, Haroun-al-Raschid, was greatly pleased with the tale of the blind man and the dervish. When it was over, he turned to the young man who had mistreated his horse and asked his name as well. The young man answered that he was called Sidi-Nouman.

“Sidi-Nouman,” said the Caliph, “I have watched horses being broken all my life, and I have broken them myself, but I have never seen a horse broken as savagely as you did it yesterday. Everyone who watched was outraged and blamed you loudly. I myself was so angry that I very nearly revealed who I was and put a stop to it on the spot. Still, you don’t look like a cruel man, and I would like to believe you didn’t act this way without a reason. I am told it was not the first time, and that every day you can be seen whipping and spurring your horse, so I want to get to the bottom of the matter. Tell me the whole truth, and hide nothing.”

Sidi-Nouman changed color when he heard this, and he grew flustered, but he saw clearly that there was no escape. So he threw himself down before the Caliph’s throne and tried to obey, but the words stuck in his throat and he stayed silent.

The Caliph, though used to being obeyed at once, guessed something of what was going on in the young man’s mind and tried to put him at ease. “Sidi-Nouman,” he said, “don’t think of me as the Caliph, but only as a friend who would like to hear your story. If there is anything in it you are afraid might offend me, take heart, for I pardon you in advance. So speak openly and without fear, as to someone who knows and loves you.”
The Caliph’s kindness put Sidi-Nouman at ease, and at last he began his story.

“Commander of the Faithful,” he said, “I am dazzled by the splendor of Your Highness’s presence, but I will do what I can to satisfy your wish. I am far from perfect, yet I am not cruel by nature, and I take no pleasure in breaking the law. I admit that the way I treated my horse may give Your Highness a poor opinion of me and set a bad example for others. Still, I did not punish it without cause, and I hope you will find me more deserving of pity than of punishment.”

“Commander of the Faithful, I won’t waste your time describing my birth. It is not distinguished enough to deserve Your Highness’s notice. My ancestors were careful people, and I inherited enough money to live comfortably, though not lavishly.

“With a modest fortune of my own, the only thing I still needed for happiness was a wife who would return my affection. But that blessing was not meant for me. The very day after the wedding, my bride started testing my patience in the hardest ways she could find.

“In our country, custom requires us to marry without ever seeing the person we will spend our lives with. So a man has no right to complain, as long as his wife is not truly repulsive or plainly deformed. And whatever flaws her body may have, charm and good conduct go a long way toward making up for them.

“When she had been brought to my house with the usual ceremonies, I saw my wife unveiled for the first time, and I was delighted to find that the reports of her beauty had not misled me. I began married life in high spirits, with every hope of happiness.

“The next day a grand dinner was served for the two of us, but my wife did not come, so I told a servant to fetch her. She still did not appear, and I waited impatiently for some time. Finally she came into the room, took her place at the table, and plates of rice were put in front of us.

“I ate mine with a spoon, as one naturally does. But I was amazed to see that my wife did nothing of the kind. She took a little case from her pocket, picked out a long pin, and used it to carry her rice to her mouth one grain at a time.

“‘Amina,’ I cried in astonishment, ‘is this how you eat rice at home? Do you do it because your appetite is so small, or are you counting the grains so that you never eat more than a certain number? If it is thrift, and you want to teach me not to be wasteful, you needn’t worry. We will never ruin ourselves that way! Our fortune is large enough for all our needs. So, dear Amina, don’t hold yourself back. Eat as much as you like, as I do!’

“After such affectionate words I expected a cheerful reply. But Amina said nothing at all. She went on picking at her rice as before, with longer and longer pauses between grains. She ignored the other dishes, and every now and then she simply put a bread crumb in her mouth, hardly enough to feed a sparrow.

“Her stubbornness annoyed me, but I tried to excuse her to myself. Perhaps she had never been used to eating with men, I thought, and her family had taught her to be modest and reserved in front of her husband. Or perhaps she had already eaten, or meant to eat later in her own rooms. So I paid no more attention, and when I had finished I left the room, privately very irritated by her strange behavior.

“The same thing happened at supper, and at every meal we shared for the whole next day. Clearly no woman could live on two or three crumbs of bread and a few grains of rice, and I decided to find out how and when she got her food. I pretended not to notice anything she did, hoping that she would gradually grow used to me and be friendlier. But I soon saw that this hope was completely in vain.

“One night I lay with my eyes shut, looking for all the world like a man fast asleep, when Amina got up softly and dressed without making the slightest sound. I couldn’t imagine where she was going, and my curiosity was so strong that I decided to follow her. As soon as she was dressed, she slipped quietly out of the room.

“The moment the curtain fell behind her, I threw a cloak over my shoulders and pushed my feet into a pair of slippers. Looking through a lattice that opened onto the courtyard, I saw her going out through the street door, which she carefully left open.

“The moon was bright, so I had no trouble keeping her in sight until she entered a cemetery not far from the house. There I hid in the shadow of the wall and crouched down carefully. I had hardly hidden myself when I saw my wife coming toward me with a ghoul. Your Highness knows these demons: they roam the country, make their lairs in abandoned buildings, and leap out at unwary travelers to eat their flesh. When no living person comes their way, they go to the cemeteries and feed on the dead.

“I was nearly struck dumb with horror at the sight of my wife with this hideous female ghoul. They passed right by me without noticing. They dug up a corpse that had been buried that very day, then sat on the edge of the grave to enjoy their dreadful meal, chatting quietly and cheerfully all the while, though I was too far away to hear what they said. When they had finished, they threw the body back into the grave and heaped the earth over it. I made no attempt to disturb them. I hurried back to the house, careful to leave the door open as I had found it, got back into bed and pretended to be sound asleep.
“A little while later Amina came in as quietly as she had gone out. She undressed and slipped into bed, apparently pleased with herself for how cleverly she had carried off her outing.

“As you can imagine, after such a scene I couldn’t sleep for a long time. At the first call to prayer I dressed and went to the mosque. But even prayer did not calm my troubled spirit, and I could not face my wife until I had decided what to do about her. So I spent the morning wandering from garden to garden, turning over different plans for forcing her to give up her horrible habits. I thought of using violence to make her submit, but I was reluctant to be unkind to her. And I had a feeling that gentle means were more likely to work. A little calmer, I turned for home and arrived about dinnertime.

“As soon as I came in, Amina ordered dinner, and we sat down together. As usual, she kept picking at a few grains of rice, and I resolved to speak to her at once about what weighed so heavily on my heart.

“‘Amina,’ I said, as calmly as I could, ‘you must have guessed how surprised I was when, the day after our wedding, you refused to eat anything but a few scraps of rice, and behaved in a way that would have deeply wounded most husbands. Still, I was patient with you. I only tried to tempt your appetite with the finest dishes I could think of, and it was all for nothing. And yet, Amina, it seems to me that there are some among them just as sweet to the taste as the flesh of a corpse?’”

“The words were hardly out of my mouth when Amina, who understood at once that I had followed her to the graveyard, flew into a rage worse than any I have ever seen. Her face turned purple, her eyes seemed about to burst from her head, and she actually foamed at the mouth.

“I watched her in terror, wondering what would come next, but never guessing where her fury would end. She seized a vessel of water that stood nearby, dipped her hand into it, and muttered some words I could not catch. Then she sprinkled the water on my face and screamed like a madwoman:
“‘Wretch, take the reward for your prying, and become a dog!’”

“The words had barely left her mouth when I knew, without feeling any change come over me, that I was no longer a man. The shock and surprise were so great, since I had no idea Amina was a sorceress, that I never thought of running. I stood rooted to the spot while Amina grabbed a stick and began to beat me. Her blows were so heavy that I only wonder they did not kill me on the spot. But they shook me out of my daze, and I bolted into the courtyard with Amina right behind me, lunging wildly at me, and I was not quick enough to dodge every blow. At last she grew tired of chasing me, or else some new trick occurred to her that would bring me a swift and painful death. She opened the gate to the street, meaning to crush me as I went through. Dog though I was, I saw what she intended, and the sheer danger sharpened my wits. I timed my dash so well that I got through, and only the tip of my tail was caught when she slammed the gate.

“I was safe, but my tail hurt terribly, and I yelped and howled so loudly all down the street that the other dogs came and attacked me, which made things no better. To get away from them, I ran into a cookshop that sold tongues and sheep’s heads.

“At first the owner was very kind. He drove off the other dogs that were still at my heels, while I crept into the darkest corner. But though I was safe for the moment, I was not meant to stay long under his protection. He was one of those people who think all dogs are unclean, and that all the washing in the world can hardly cleanse you after touching one. So once my enemies had gone off to hunt other prey, he tried to coax me out of my corner and force me into the street. But I refused to leave my hole, and I spent the night asleep, which I badly needed after the pain Amina had given me.

“I don’t want to tire Your Highness with the sad thoughts that filled me after my change of shape. But you may be interested to hear that the next morning my host went out early to do his marketing and came back loaded with the sheep’s heads, tongues and trotters he would sell that day. The smell of meat drew hungry dogs from all over the neighborhood, and they gathered at the door, begging for scraps. I crept out of my corner and stood with them.

“Though he disliked dogs as unclean animals, my protector was a kind-hearted man. Knowing I had eaten nothing since the day before, he threw me bigger and better pieces than the ones the other dogs got. When I had finished, I tried to go back into the shop, but he wouldn’t allow it. He stood so firmly in the doorway with a stout stick that I had to give up and look for another home.

“A few steps further on was a baker’s shop, and its master seemed to be a cheerful, good-humored man. He was eating his breakfast at that moment, and though I gave no sign of hunger, he threw me a piece of bread right away. Before gobbling it up, as most dogs do, I bowed my head and wagged my tail to thank him. He understood, and smiled warmly. I didn’t really want the bread at all, but I felt it would be rude to refuse, so I ate it slowly, to show him I was only doing it out of politeness. He understood that too, and seemed quite willing to let me stay in his shop. So I sat down facing the door, to show that I asked only for his protection. He gave it, and even encouraged me to come into the house itself, giving me a corner to sleep in where I would be out of everyone’s way.

“The kindness this excellent man heaped on me was far greater than anything I could ever have expected. He was always affectionate in the way he treated me, and I shared his breakfast, dinner and supper, while I gave him all the gratitude and devotion he deserved.

“I sat with my eyes fixed on him, and he never left the house without me at his heels. If I happened to be asleep when he was getting ready to go out, and didn’t notice, he would call, ‘Rufus, Rufus!’ since that was the name he had given me.

“Some weeks went by like this. Then one day a woman came in to buy bread. In paying, she put down several coins, and one of them was counterfeit. The baker noticed and refused to take it, asking for another in its place. The woman, for her part, refused to take it back, insisting it was perfectly good, but the baker would have nothing to do with it. ‘It’s such a poor imitation,’ he cried at last, ‘that even my dog wouldn’t be fooled. Here, Rufus! Rufus!’ At the sound of his voice I jumped onto the counter. The baker threw the coins down in front of me and said, ‘Find out if there is a bad coin.’ I looked at each in turn, then laid my paw on the false one, glancing at my master to point it out.

“The baker had only been joking, of course, and he was amazed at my cleverness. The woman, finally convinced that the man was telling the truth, handed over another coin in its place. After she left, my master was so pleased that he told all the neighbors what I had done, and made far more of it than there really was.
“The neighbors, quite naturally, refused to believe his story. They tested me several times with all the bad money they could gather, but I never failed the test.

“Soon the shop was full from morning till night with people who, on the pretext of buying bread, had come to see whether I was as clever as they had heard. The baker did a roaring trade, and admitted I was worth my weight in gold to him.

“Naturally, plenty of people were jealous of his thriving trade, and many traps were laid for me, so he never dared let me out of his sight. One day a woman I had never seen in the shop came in to buy bread like everyone else. As usual I was lying on the counter. She put down six coins in front of me, and one of them was counterfeit. I spotted it straight away and laid my paw on it, looking up at the woman as I did. ‘Yes,’ she said, nodding. ‘You’re right, that’s the one.’ She stood studying me for a long while, then paid for her bread and left the shop, signaling to me to follow her without being seen.

“My mind was always fixed on finding some way to throw off the spell that bound me, and the way this woman had looked at me made me think she might have guessed what had happened to me. I was not wrong. Still, I let her get a little way off and only stood at the door watching her. She turned around, and when she saw I hadn’t moved, she beckoned to me again.
“All this time the baker was busy at his oven and had forgotten about me, so I slipped out quietly and ran after the woman.

“Her house was a good distance away. When we got there she opened the door and said to me, ‘Come in, come in. You will never regret following me.’ Once I was inside she bolted the door and led me into a large room, where a beautiful young woman sat at her embroidery. ‘Daughter,’ my guide cried, ‘I’ve brought you the baker’s famous dog, the one that can tell good money from bad. When I first heard about him, remember, I told you he had to be a man, turned into a dog by magic. Today I went to the baker’s to test the story for myself, and I talked the dog into following me here. Now what do you say?’

“‘You’re right, mother,’ the girl answered. She got up and dipped her hand into a bowl of water, then sprinkled it over me and said, ‘If you were born a dog, stay a dog; but if you were born a man, let this water give you back your true shape.’ In an instant the spell was gone. The dog’s form vanished as if it had never existed, and a man stood in front of her.

“Overwhelmed with gratitude at being freed, I threw myself at her feet and kissed the hem of her dress. ‘How can I thank you for your kindness to a stranger, and for what you have done for me? From now on I am your slave. Do with me as you wish!’
“Then, to explain how I had come to be turned into a dog, I told her my whole story. I ended by thanking the mother for the happiness she had given me.

“‘Sidi-Nouman,’ the daughter replied, ‘don’t speak any more of what you owe us. Knowing we have helped you is payment enough. Let’s talk about Amina, your wife. I knew her before she married. I knew she was a magician, and she knew I had studied the same art under the same teacher. We often met at the same baths, but we disliked each other and never tried to be friends. As for you, it isn’t enough that your spell has been broken. She must be punished for her wickedness. Please wait a moment here with my mother,’ she added quickly. ‘I’ll be back soon.’
“Left alone with the mother, I told her again how grateful I was, to her as well as to her daughter.

“‘My daughter,’ she told me, ‘is as skilled a magician as Amina herself, as you can see, but you would be amazed at how much good she does with her knowledge. That is why I have never stood in her way; otherwise I would have put a stop to it long ago.’ As she was speaking, her daughter came back in, holding a small bottle.

“‘Sidi-Nouman,’ she said, ‘the books I’ve just looked in tell me that Amina is out at the moment but will be back at any time. They also show me that in front of the servants she is pretending to be very worried about your absence. She has put about a story that while you were at dinner with her, you suddenly remembered some urgent business and rushed out of the house without closing the door. A dog wandered in through it, she says, and she had to drive it out with a stick. So go home at once and wait in your room for Amina to come back. When she arrives, go down and meet her, and in her shock she will try to run off. Then have this bottle ready and throw the water in it over her, saying boldly, “Receive the reward of your crimes.” That is all I have to tell you.’

“Everything happened just as the young magician had said it would. I had been in my house only a few minutes when Amina came back, and as she came toward me I stepped in front of her with the water in my hand. She gave a loud cry and turned for the door, but it was too late. I had already thrown the water in her face and spoken the magic words. Amina vanished, and in her place stood the horse you saw me beating yesterday.
“That, Commander of the Faithful, is my story. Now that you have heard my reasons for what I did, may I hope that your Highness will not think this wicked woman has been treated too harshly?”

“Sidi-Nouman,” the Caliph answered, “your story is certainly a strange one, and nothing can be said in your wife’s defense. But without condemning how you have treated her, I ask you to think how much she must suffer from being turned into an animal, and I hope you will let that be punishment enough. I will not order you to make the young magician find a way to give your wife back her human form, because I know that once women like her start doing evil they never stop, and I would only call down on your head a revenge far worse than the one you have already suffered.”
